content.topicNotes: The 12-Hour Clock There are 24 hours in a day which are split up into two 12 hour periods. These are split into am (the 12 hours before midday) and pm (the 12 hours after midday). Hands of a clock The shorter hand shows how many hours have passed. This is shown by the numbers on the clock. The longer hand shows how many minutes have passed. The gap between each number is 5 minutes O'clock If the minute (longer) hand points to 12, you say it is o'clock. E.g. 3 o'clock Half past If the minute (longer) hand points to 6, you say it is half past the hour. This is because half the hour has passed. E.g. Half past 3. Quarter past If the minute (longer) hand points to 3, you say it is quarter past the hour. This is because a quarter of the hour has passed. E.g. quarter past 3. Quarter to If the minute (longer) hand points to 9, you say it is quarter to the upcoming hour. This is because a quarter of the hour is left until a new hour is reached. E.g. quarter to 3.

content.topicNotes: The 12-Hour Clock The minute hand shows the exact minute past the hour. Sections of a clock Each number represents a different number of minutes. content.topicNotes: 24-Hour Clock The 24-hour clock doesn't use am or pm. Instead, it gives the hour of the day starting from 0 at the start of the day and running up to 24 at the end of the day. 12 is at midday. In the morning (am) Times before midday are the same in a 24-hour or 12-hour format. The only difference is you don't need the "am" when using the 24-hour clock. E.g. 10:40 am is 10:40 in the 24-hour clock. E.g. 09:20 am is 09:20 in the 24-hour clock. Midday Midday is the same in the 24-hour and 12-hour clock with the "pm" removed. Midday in the 12-hour clock is 12:00 pm or 12:00 noon. Midday in the 24-hour clock is 12:00. In the afternoon (pm) 1 o'clock in the afternoon is 1:00 pm in the 12-hour clock. 1 o'clock in the afternoon is 13:00 in the 24-hour clock. This is because the 24-hour clock carries on counting from 12 noon. Examples 6 o'clock in the afternoon is 18:00 in the 24-hour clock. 4 o'clock in the morning is 04:00 in the 24-hour clock. 12 midnight is 00:00 in the 24-hour clock. 10 o'clock in the evening is 22:00 in the 24-hour clock. Uses of the 24-hour clock The 24-hour clock is often used on timetables. E.g. bus, train and plane timetables You'll also normally see the time on your phone in a 24-hour clock.

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Alternate segment theorem The angle between a tangent and a chord is always equal to the angle at the circumference of any triangle formed from the chord. Proof Draw in a diameter from the point where the tangent touches. Connect it to the other end of the chord. Proof continued Using ‘radius and tangent meet at a right angle’ we get a right angle where the diameter meets the tangent. Using ‘angle in a semicircle is 90°’ we get that the angle at the other end of the chord is a right angle too. Proof continued We find that the angle at the bottom of the diameter is the same as x. Using ‘angles in same segment’ we get that x = y.

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Angle at centre is double the angle at the circumference Proof Split the shape into two isosceles triangles and label the angles. The angle at the centre is 360° - x - y and the angle at the circumference is a + b. Proof continued Since the angles in a triangle add up to 180°: a = 1⁄2(180° - y), b = 1⁄2(180° - x) So angle at circumference = a + b = 1⁄2(360° - x - y) = 1⁄2 × angle at centre.

content.topicNotes: Circle Theorems Angle in a semicircle is 90° Proof Split the triangle into two triangles which are both isosceles since they both have two sides which are radii. Mark one of the angles at the centre x. Proof continued y = 1⁄2(180° - x) since the triangle is isosceles and all angles add up to 180°. Similarly z = 1⁄2(180° - (180° - x)) = 1⁄2x Therefore the angle at the circumference is z + y = 1⁄2 × 180° = 90° as required. Alternative proof Alternatively, using the previous theorem we see that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. So 180° is twice the angle at the circumference so the angle is 90°.

Exterior angles If you extend the side of a polygon outside the shape then the exterior angle is the angle between the extended line and the adjacent edge. The exterior angles add up to 360°. content.topicNotes: Applying Congruent Triangles Congruent triangles can be used in simple proofs. Proofs If two isosceles triangles have congruent sides, you can deduce that they will also have congruent angles. Similarly, if two isosceles triangles have congruent angles, you can deduce that they will have congruent sides. Question Step 1 Construct 2 right angled triangles. Step 2 Side PS and side PQ are congruent. Triangle PQR and PSR share side PR. Therefore angle QPR and angle SPR are congruent. Step 3 Using the 'side-angle-side' theory, we have proven that: Side PS and PQ are congruent, side PR and PR are congruent, and that angle QPR and angle PSR are congruent. Therefore triangle PQR and PSR are congruent. Step 4 Therefore, angle PQS is congruent to angle PSQ.

content.topicNotes: Combining Transformations It is possible to combine the notation for reflection (M), rotation (R), translation (T) and enlargement (E). Combining transformations You can combine the notation to perform two transformations at a time. E.g. You could write ER(a) = b to rotate shape a and then enlarge it to give shape b. Examples To enlarge shape a and then translate it to give shape b, we could write TE(a) = b. To rotate shape a and then reflect it to give shape b, we could write MR(a) = b. Which one first? The first transformation you do is the one closest to the brackets. You then work away from the brackets and do any transformations in order. RERT(a) = b would be a translation of a, then a rotation, then an enlargement and finally another rotation to give b. Invariant points Invariant points are points that don't change following a transformation. Invariant points can be left out of this notation as it does not affect the result.

E.g. 5 × 2 is the same as 2 × 5 E.g. 100 × 6 is the same as 6 × 100 Matrices Matrices do NOT generally obey the Commutative Law because matrix multiplication is NOT commutative. Changing the order of multiplication between two matrices will give a different answer (usually). Example Look at the example above that shows that matrices are NOT commutative. Identity and Zero Matrices The identity and zero matrices have particular structures and properties. The identity matrix The only time that you get the same answer when you change the order of multiplication between two matrices is when one of the matrices is the identity matrix. The identity matrix cont. The identity matrix is a matrix with the following properties: The matrix has square dimensions. This is referred to as an n × n matrix where n is the number of rows or columns. All values in the matrix are 0 except for the main diagonal values (top left to bottom right) which are 1. The zero matrix The zero matrix is a matrix the consists entirely of zeros. The zero matrix can take any dimensions. Multiplying by the zero matrix will produce a zero matrix. Adding the zero matrix will not change a matrix.

content.topicNotes: Describing Reflections Transformation can be used to describe how a shape or point moves on coordinate axes. Describing a reflection A reflection is described using a mirror line. The mirror line is often described using an equation. E.g. x = 1, y = 0, y = x The mirror line can be found by finding the line that is exactly in the middle of the corresponding (matching) points in the object and image. Describing a translation A translation is described by describing the movement in the x and y directions. Translations can be described using column vectors, e.g. $$\Big({\large{3}\atop{5}}\Big)$$. The top number describes how the object is translated across. The top number describes how the object is translated up or down. Column vectors A positive number translates an object in a positive direction (up or to the right). A negative number translates an object in a negative direction (down or to the left). Finding a translation You can find a translation by looking at how a point on the object has moved to get to a corresponding (matching) point on the image.

content.topicNotes: Describing Transformations Transformation can be used to describe how a shape or point moves on coordinate axes. Object and image The original shape or point before a transformation is known as the object. The new shape or point after a transformation is known as the image. Describing a rotation An angle of rotation and a centre of rotation are required to describe a rotation. The angle of rotation tells you how much the object rotates by. You can often tell the angle of rotation by comparing the orientation (way round) of the object and image. The centre of rotation tells you where the rotation centres around. Angle of rotation Look at the orientation to work out the angle of rotation. Centre of rotation Find the centre of rotation using tracing paper. Draw around the object and place your pencil where you think the centre of rotation is. Centre of rotation cont. Use trial and error until you rotate the object on the tracing paper and it makes the image. This takes a lot of practice to get good at but it gets easier the more you try it.

content.topicNotes: Describing Transformations with Matrices Matrices can be used to describe the four transformations: translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement. Coordinates as vertex matrices Vertex matrices can be used to describe a set of coordinates. The number of rows of the vertex matrix tells you how many dimensions there are (i.e. 2 rows when there are only x and y coordinates). Each column is a different coordinate. E.g. the coordinates (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), (7, 8) can be displayed in the vertex matrix above. Coordinates as vertex matrices 2 The general rule is that for each coordinate, (xn, yn), a vertex matrix can be written as above. Translations with matrices Translations can be described using column matrices, e.g. $$\Big[{\large{3}\atop{-1}}\Big]$$. The top number describes how the object is translated across. The top number describes how the object is translated up or down. Translations with matrices 2 A positive number translates an object in a positive direction (up or to the right). A negative number translates an object in a negative direction (down or to the left). Transformations with Matrices Matrices can be used to describe the four transformations: translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement. Reflection with matrices You can reflect the coordinates in a vertex matrix in particular mirror lines by multiplying one of the matrices above by the vertex matrix (in that order). Rotate with matrices You can rotate the coordinates in a vertex matrix about the origin by multiplying one of the matrices above by the vertex matrix (in that order). Enlargement with matrices You can enlarge the coordinates in a vertex matrix by a particular scale factor about the origin by multiplying a scalar value by the vertex matrix (in that order).

content.topicNotes: Directed Line Segments Directed line segments have two key features: direction and magnitude (size). Directed line segments A directed line segment shows a vector between two points. A directed line segment has a start point and end point. Direction and magnitude A directed line segment always has a fixed direction and magnitude (size). Directed line segments are equivalent (the same) if they have the same direction and magnitude (size). The same directed line segments can start and end in different positions but must have the same direction and magnitude (size). Negative vectors Negative vectors have the same magnitude (size) as the positive of that vector. Negative vectors have the opposite direction to the positive of that vector. Magnitude of Vectors Vectors have a magnitude (size) and direction. The magnitude of a vector can be calculated from the column vector. Calculating the magnitude You can use Pythagoras' theorem to calculate the magnitude of a vector ($$\large{x}\atop{y}$$). The magnitude of a vector $$({\large{x}\atop{y}})$$ is $$\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$$. Vector notation You will need to be careful when writing vectors in your exam. Vectors will be printed on the exam as $$\vec{AB}$$ or a. The magnitude of a vector will be shown using modulus signs. I.e. magnitude of $$\vec{AB}$$ = |$$\vec{AB}$$| I.e. magnitude of a = |a| Using vector notation In your exam, you will need to show the examiner that you know the difference between the vector a and the letter a. There are two ways to do this: Using an arrow above the vector, e.g. $$\vec{AB}$$ Underlining the letter, e.g. $$\underline{a}$$

content.topicNotes: The Dot Product The dot product is needed to multiply two matrices together. The dot product involves a mixture of multiplication and addition. We will explore the dot product using an example. The dot product The dot product involves multiplying members in each row of the first matrix with matching members of the second matrix. Start by identifying the first row of the first matrix and the first column of the second matrix. The dot product cont. Then multiply the numbers in matching positions. For example: The 1st number in the 1st matrix's 1st row multiplied by 1st number in the 2nd matrix's 1st column. The 2nd number in the 1st matrix's 1st row multiplied by 2nd number in the 2nd matrix's 1st column. The 3rd number in the 1st matrix's 1st row multiplied by 3rd number in the 2nd matrix's 1st column. Add the values Those values are then added together to give the number that goes in the 1st row and 1st column in the answer. Repeat We then do the same with the 1st row in the 1st matrix and the 2nd column in the 2nd matrix. This will give the number that goes in the 1st row and 2nd column in the answer. Repeat again Do the same with the 2nd row in the 1st matrix and the 1st column in the 2nd matrix. This will give the number that goes in the 2nd row and 1st column in the answer. And again Do the same with the 2nd row in the 1st matrix and the 2nd column in the 2nd matrix. This will give the number that goes in the 2nd row and 2nd column in the answer. Keep going Do the same with the remaining rows and columns until you complete the 3 × 2 matrix. 67 comes from (5 × 8) + (9 × 3)

content.topicNotes: Drawing Graphs Graphs can be plotted (drawn) from data displayed in tables. Graphs Graphs can be used to show the relationship between two variables (something that can change). E.g. you could plot a graph to show the relationship between speed and time. E.g. you could plot a graph to show the relationship between the number of Instagram posts and the number of followers. Equipment A sharp pencil should be used to plot (draw) graphs. Points on a graph should be marked with a cross (×). Tables Your data will be displayed in the form of a table. Each data point can be read by looking at each row. Axes The independent variable should go on the x-axis. This is the variable that is fixed for some data. In this example, the independent variable is time. This is a fixed value for each video. The dependent variable should go on the y-axis. This is the variable that can change depending on various conditions. In this example, the independent variable is the number of likes because it can vary for each video. Plotting a graph The cross goes where the value for the x-axis meets the value for the y-axis. Complete this for each piece of data you want to plot. Remembering the x and y-axes There's a helpful way to remember which axis is the x-axis and which axis is the y-axis. Y to the sky The y-axis points upwards (to the sky). X is a cross X goes across the place (and the letter x also looks like a cross)

content.topicNotes: Enlargement with Negative Scale Factors When asked to enlarge an image with a negative scale factor, the resulting image is 'upside down'. This is because the image is on the opposite side of the centre of enlargement. Step 1 Identify the scale factor and the centre of enlargement. Step 2 Enlarge the original image. If A has negative x and y coordinates, B will have positive x and y coordinates. Example explained Because the scale factor is -2, B is twice the size of A. The coordinates for the image are switched. In this case, the coordinates for points P, Q and R are negative. So points P', Q', R' are all positive. Scale Factor Enlargement If a shape is enlarged by a scale factor, S, all the lengths in that shape will be multiplied by S. Fractional scale factors When enlarging something by a fractional scale factor, it will actually get smaller. E.g. Enlarging a 10 cm line by scale factor $$ \frac{1}{2}$$ will multiply the length by $$ \frac{1}{2}$$. This means that the line will be 5 cm long after the enlargement. Negative scale factors Negative scale factors still enlarge a shape by multiplying the lengths by scale factor S. E.g. Enlarging a 10 cm line by scale factor −2 will multiply the length by −2. But, the line won't be −20 cm long because length is a scalar quantity and, therefore, cannot negative. This means that the line will be 20 cm long after the enlargement. Scale Factors with Area and Volume To work out the area and volume of a shape after enlargement, consider that an enlargement occurs in every dimension. Length Enlarging a length by scale factor S will multiply the length by S. E.g. Enlarge a line with a length of 5 cm by scale factor 2.5 × 2 = 10 cm The enlarged line will have a length of 10 cm. Area Enlarging an area by scale factor S will multiply the area by S2. This is because the lengths of both dimensions of the 2D shape will be enlarged by a scale factor S. E.g. Enlarge a square with an area of 5 cm2 by scale factor 2.5 × 22 = 20 cm2 The enlarged square will have an area of 20 cm2. Volume Enlarging a volume by scale factor S will multiply the volume by S3. This is because the lengths of all dimensions of the 3D shape will be enlarged by a scale factor S. E.g. Enlarge a cube with an volume of 5 cm3 by scale factor 2.5 × 23 = 40 cm3 The enlarged cube will have a volume of 40 cm3.

content.topicNotes: Equation of a Parallel Line You can use the gradient of a parallel line and a known point on the line to work out its equation. Gradient The gradient of the unknown line will be the same as the gradient of a parallel line. y-intercept The y-intercept is where the straight line intercepts (crosses) the y-axis. The y-intercept of an unknown straight line can be worked out using the other known values. Example question A line is parallel to the line y = 3x − 2 and goes through the point (1, 4). What is the equation of this straight line? Example answer We know that the line is parallel so the gradient of the unknown line must be 3. We can write this as y = 3x + c Example answer cont. We know the line goes through (1 , 4). When x = 1, y = 4 in the equation. Substitute in the values for x and y into the equation. 4 = (3 × 1) + c Example answer cont. Solve the equation to find c. 4 = 3 + c c = 1 Rewrite the equation using the values of m = 3 and c = 1 to give the equation of the parallel line that goes through (1, 4). y = 3x + 1

content.topicNotes: Equation of a Parallel Line You can use the gradient of a perpendicular line and a known point on the line to work out its equation. Gradient The gradient of the unknown line will be the negative reciprocal of the perpendicular line. E.g. the negative reciprocal of 6 = −$$\large\frac{1}{6}$$ y-intercept The y-intercept is where the straight line intercepts (crosses) the y-axis. The y-intercept of an unknown straight line can be worked out using the other known values. Example question A line is perpendicular to the line y = 4x + 2 and goes through the point (8, 4). What is the equation of this straight line? Example answer We know that the line is perpendicular so the gradient of the unknown line the negative reciprocal of 4 = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$. We can write this as y = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$x + c Example answer cont. We know the perpendicular line goes through (8 , 4). When x = 8, y = 4 in the equation. Substitute in the values for x and y into the equation. 4 = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$(8) + c Example answer cont. Solve the equation to find c. 4 = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$(8) + c c = 6 Rewrite the equation using the values of m = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$ and c = 6 to give the equation of the perpendicular line that goes through (8, 4). y = −$$\large\frac{1}{4}$$x + 6

content.topicNotes: Estimating Area Under a Graph Straight lines only - exact calculation To calculate the area under a graph, split the area into trapeziums and rectangles and work out the area of each section. Use the formula: Area (Trapezium) = 1⁄2 × base × (a + b) Where a and b are the sides of the trapezium. Curved line - estimate If the graph is not made up of straight lines you can estimate the area by splitting the graph approximately into trapeziums and doing the same calculation. Overestimate or underestimate An area estimate is an overestimate when the trapeziums are above the curve and an underestimate when the trapeziums are below the curve. content.topicNotes: Estimating Gradient The gradient of a graph can be estimated at any point. The gradient of a graph tells you the rate of change in the graph, i.e. how steep the graph is. Gradient The gradient of a graph tells you how steep it is. You can measure the gradient by drawing a tangent to a curve. A tangent is any straight line that just touches a curve. It does not cross the curve. Estimating the gradient Once you have drawn a tangent, you can work out its gradient to make an estimate for the gradient of the curve at that point. You calculate the gradient of the tangent by working out the $$\large \frac{change;in;y}{change;in;x}$$. Estimating the gradient example What is the gradient of the curve when $$x$$ = 1? Example $$x$$ = 1 at (1, 1). The tangent has been drawn in orange. Example cont. As $$x$$ increases by 1, $$y$$ increases by 2. Gradient = $$\large \frac{change;in;y}{change;in;x}$$ = $$\large \frac{2}{1}$$ = 2

content.topicNotes: Angle Properties of Irregular Polygons Irregular polygons are polygons that have varying angle sizes and side lengths. Regular vs irregular polygons All polygons are named based on the number of sides they have. Some polygons have all angles and side lengths the same. These are called regular polygons. Some polygons have angles of different sizes and sides of different lengths. These are called irregular polygons. Exterior angles The exterior angles of all polygons add up to 360°. This is true for both regular and irregular polygons. Calculating an interior angle An exterior angle can be used to calculate the interior angle inside the polygon. You can calculate the interior angle of a polygon by using the fact that angles on a straight line add up to 180°. E.g. if the exterior angle is 40° then the interior angle will be: 180° − 40° = 140°

content.topicNotes: Factorising Quadratics We can factorise quadratics in the form ax² + bx + c when a = 1. To factorise x² + 2x - 8: Find pairs of numbers which multiply to give (-8) Select the pair which also adds to give 2 These numbers multiply to give (-8) and add to give 2 Write these two numbers in the brackets Check your answer by expanding the brackets Factorising Quadratics Follow these steps to factorise an expression of the form ax² + bx + c where a is not 1. We use 2x² + 10x + 8 as an example. Step 1 Work out the initial set of brackets. The coefficients of x must multiply to give a (a = 2 in this example). Step 2 Find pairs of numbers that multiply to give c (8 in this case). Step 3 Trial and error until you find a combination that works. Try each pair both ways round (e.g. 2 in the 2x bracket or in the x bracket) and with different signs until you find a combination that results in the correct x coefficient in the expansion. Step 4 Always expand to check your answer works. Factorising Factorising is when we put an equation into brackets. Like this present being wrapped.

content.topicNotes: Differentiation The derivative of a function can be worked out through a process called differentiation. Differentiation There are different ways to display the derivative of a function. If your equation starts with y =, then the derivative of the equation is $$\large\frac{dy}{dx}$$. If your function starts with f($$x$$) =, then the derivative of the equation is f'($$x$$). The exam may also ask you to find the rate of change, the gradient of the tangent or to differentiate a function. General rule To differentiate a whole equation/function, each term should be differentiated individually. The general rule for differentiating a term is: f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 Examples f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = $$x$$3 → f'($$x$$) = 3$$x$$2 f($$x$$) = 2$$x$$3 → f'($$x$$) = 6$$x$$2 f($$x$$) = 6$$x$$ → f'($$x$$) = 6 (remember f($$x$$) = 6$$x$$ is the same as 6$$x$$1) f($$x$$) = 3$$x$$4 → f'($$x$$) = 12$$x$$3 f($$x$$) = 9 → f'($$x$$) = 0 (remember f($$x$$) = 9 is the same as 9$$x$$0) Example 1 with multiple terms For each term in an expression, use f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = $$x$$3 + 2$$x$$2 + 7$$x$$ f'($$x$$) = 3$$x$$2 + 4$$x$$ + 7 Example 1 with multiple terms For each term in an expression, use f($$x$$) = $$ax^n$$ → f'($$x$$) = $$nax$$ $$n$$−1 f($$x$$) = 3$$x$$4 + 5$$x$$3 + 4$$x$$2 f'($$x$$) = 12$$x$$3 + 15$$x$$2 + 8$$x$$

content.topicNotes: How do you find the Centre and Radius of a Circle? To find the centre and radius of a circle from its expanded equation, we need to complete the square. What is the expanded equation of a circle? If we expand the general equation of a circle with centre $$(a,b)$$ and radius $$r$$ we get: $$(x - a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2$$ $$x^2 -2ax + a^2 +y^2 -2by +b^2=r^2 $$ $$x^2 +y^2 -2ax -2by +a^2+b^2-r^2 = 0$$ What is the expanded equation of a circle? If we make the substitutions: $$a = -f$$ $$b = -g$$ $$a^2+b^2-r^2= c$$ Then the expanded form of the equation of a circle is given by: $$x^2+y^2 +2fx +2gy+c = 0$$ How do you find the centre and radius of a circle? If the equation of a circle is in the expanded form, we can complete the square and find the circle in the general form: $$(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 = r^2$$. The centre of the circle is at the point $$(a,b)$$ and the radius is of length $$r$$. Example What is the centre and radius of the circle with equation $$x^2 + y^2-4x-6y+4 = 0$$? Group together $$x$$ and $$y$$ terms To begin, we group together the terms containing $$x$$ and the terms containing $$y$$: $$x^2 -4x + y^2 - 6y + 4 = 0$$ Complete the square for terms containing $$x$$ We then complete the square for the $$x$$ terms alone: $$x^2 -4x = (x-2)^2 -4$$ Complete the square for terms containing $$7$$ We then complete the square for the $$y$$ terms alone: $$y^2 -6y = (y-3)^2 -9$$ Substitute in We then substitute these back into the equation: $$(x-2)^2 - 4 + (y-3)^2 -9 +4=0$$ Simplify Simplifying the constants gives: $$(x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2 -9 = 0$$ Then adding 9 (which is 32) to each side, we get the equation of the circle in its general form: $$(x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2 = 3^2$$ Inspect Comparing this to the general form of the equation, we can see that the centre of the circle is at the point (2,3) and the radius is equal to 3.

content.topicNotes: Gradient and y-intercept of a Line A line y = mx + c has gradient m and y-intercept c. y-intercept The point where a line crosses the y-axis is called the y-intercept. Gradient To calculate the gradient (slope) of a line, use 2 co-ordinates (A and B): gradient = change in y ÷ change in x where change in y = (yA - yB) and change in x = (xA - xB) Finding the Equation of a Line From a Graph We can calculate the equation of a line if we have two points on the line or one point and the gradient. Given two points - method To find the equation of a line between two points, first calculate the gradient m. Then substitute in one of the points into the equation and rearrange to find c. For example to find the equation of the line between (2,4) and (-1,2)... Given two points - step 1 Find the gradient: change in y = 4 - 2 = 2 change in x = 2 - (-1) = 3 so m = 2⁄3 Given two points - step 2 We know the line is y = 2⁄3x + c so substitute in x = 2 and y = 4 to find c: (4) = 2⁄3(2) + c so c = 8⁄3 Therefore the line is y = 2⁄3x + 8⁄3. Given gradient and point To find the equation of a line with a given gradient and going through a point substitute in the point to the line y = mx + c where m is the gradient you’ve been given.

content.topicNotes: Interpreting Frequency Tables Mode The modal value or class in a frequency table is simply the value or class with the highest frequency. Range The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values. When the data is grouped the range can be estimated as the difference between the highest and lowest class boundaries. Mean - ungrouped table To calculate the exact mean in an ungrouped frequency table, add a column which is ‘value × frequency’. Add up all the values in this column to get the total of all values and then divide by the sum of the frequencies to get the mean. Mean - grouped table To estimate the mean in a grouped frequency table add a column which is ‘mid-interval value’ and another column which is ‘mid-interval value × frequency’. content.topicNotes: Rounding and Accuracy If we round numbers then the accuracy of our calculation can change. The weight of a cooking pot to the nearest kilogram is 7kg. What is the range of possible weights of the pan? Lower bound is 6.5. It is smallest number that rounds up to 7 Upper bound is 7.5. Lowest number that won't round down to 7 The upper bound is 7.5 Range of possible weights Upper and Lower Bounds You need to know how to use bounds to work the higher and lower bounds of calculations with numbers that have been rounded. Upper and lower bounds of calculations To work out the upper and lower bound of a calculation, you need to work out the upper and lower bound for each value used in a calculation. You can then use these individual bounds to work out the upper and lower bounds of the calculation. Example - multiplication You are calculating the upper and lower bounds of the area of a rectangle. The height is 0.5 to 1 decimal place. The height's lower bound is 0.45 and the upper bound is 0.55. The length is 10 to 2 significant figures. The length's lower bound is 9.5 and upper bound is 10.5. Example cont. - multiplication The lower bound for the area is the smallest possible height × the smallest possible length. I.e. 0.45 × 9.5 = 4.275 The upper bound for the area is the largest possible height × the largest possible length. I.e. 0.55 × 10.5 = 5.775 Example - division You are calculating the upper and lower bounds of the speed = distance ÷ time. A car travels 30 km to 1 significant figure. The lower bound for the distance is 25 km and the upper bound is 35 km. The time is 7 hours to 1 significant figure. The lower bound of the time is 6.5 hours and the upper bound is 7.5 hours. Example cont. - division The lower bound for the speed of the car is the smallest possible distance ÷ the largest possible time. I.e. 25 ÷ 7.5 = 3.33 km/h The upper bound for the speed of the car is the largest possible distance × the smallest possible time. I.e. 35 ÷ 6.5 = 5.38 km/h

content.topicNotes: Maxima & Minima Calculus can be used to find the maximum and minimum values of physical quantities. Minima, where the function is the smallest. Turning points The gradient of a graph is equal to the derivative of the graph. -The $$x$$-coordinate of a turning point is found by setting $$f\prime(x)$$ or $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ equal to zero. It is called a turning point because the graph often changes direction at f'($$x$$) = 0. Kinematics We can use the same method to work out the maximum and minimum values of physical quantities if they are expressed as a function of time. For example, if $$v = -2t^2+t+4$$: $$\frac{dv}{dt} = -4t + 1 = 0 \rightarrow t = 0.25$$ s. $$v = -2\times0.25^2 + 0.25 + 4 = 4.38$$ m/s (2 d.p.). content.topicNotes: Perpendicular Line Through a Point It is possible to construct a perpendicular line through a point using a ruler and a pair of compasses. Perpendicular through a point A perpendicular line will be the shortest distance between a point and a line. The line will be perpendicular (at right angles to) to another line (e.g. line AB). It will also pass through a given point away from the line (e.g. point C). Step 1 Put the point of your compass on the point you want the line to go through (in this example, point C). Draw an arc that intersects (crosses) the line you want to draw a line perpendicular to (in this example, line AB). Step 2 Keep the compasses the same distance apart as in step 1. Place the point of the compass on one of the places that the arc intersects (crosses) the line AB (shown in red). Draw an arc below the line AB. Step 3 Keep the compasses the same distance apart as in the previous steps. Place the point of the compass on the other place that the arc intersects (crosses) the line AB (shown in red). Draw another arc below the line AB. It should intersect (cross) the arc you drew in the previous step. Step 4 Draw a straight line between your point (point C) and where the final two arcs intersect (cross) each other (both points are shown in red). The result The result is a line that's perpendicular to AB and goes through point C. Leave in your arcs as evidence of your working.

Sample needs to be representative When choosing a sample it is important for it to be representative of the whole population so that measurements we take in the sample can be used as estimates for the population. Random sample To choose a random sample you can assign a number to each member of the population then use a computer or a random number table or pick numbers out of a hat to choose a random selection of numbers. content.topicNotes: Simultaneous Equations Solve the simultaneous equations equations -x + 3y = 6 and 3x - 3 = 2y: Label equations Rearrange to get x and y's on one side Multiply to get same x term Add or subtract to eliminate x Simplify Simplify Find solution for y Sub solution for y back into equation 2 We could also sub the solution into equation 1 and we would get the same answer. Simplify to find x Find the solution for x Sub solutions back into equation 1 as a check This is true so we know our solutions are correct Simultaneous Equations To solve simultaneous equations, add together the 2 equations so that one of the unknowns (x, y or a etc.) cancels out. Then you can work out what one of them is. Once you know one, sub in the answer to find out the other. Simultaneous Quadratic Equations You can solve a pair of simultaneous equations where at least one contains a quadratic using the substitution method. This is where you rearrange one of the equations and substitute it into the other equation. Example Take the pair of simultaneous equations: 2x2 + y = 5 2x + y = 1 You can rearrange the second equation to get: y = 1 − 2x Substitution y = 1 − 2x can then be substituted in as an expression for y in 2x2 + y = 5. This gives 2x2 + 1 − 2x = 5 Which can be rearranged to 2x2 − 2x − 4 = 0 Solving for x You can then solve 2x2 − 2x − 4 = 0 to find values of x that satisfies the simultaneous equations. 2x2 − 2x − 4 = 0 (2x + 2)(x − 2) = 0 Therfore x = −1 and x = 2 Solving for y You then need to find out the values of y by substituting in the values x = −1 and x = 2. Solving for y when x = −1 2x + y = 1 2(−1) + y = 1 y = 3 This means x = −1 and y = 3 is one solution to the simultaneous equations. Solving for y when x = 2 2x + y = 1 2(2) + y = 1 y = −3 This means x = 2 and y = −3 is the other solution to the simultaneous equations.

Calculating the quotient When both numbers in the division calculation are negative, the quotient is positive. When one number in the division calculation is negative and the other is positive, the quotient is negative. Some tips Calculating the sum and difference: If the calculation's function (the + or −) is the same as the sign in front of the 2nd number in the equation, the answer will be positive. If the calculation's function (the + or −) is different to the sign in front of the 2nd number in the equation, the answer will be negative. Calculating the product and quotient: If the numbers in the equation are either both positive or both negative, the answer will be a positive number. Each column after that shows the running of a single train/bus. The time shown shows the time that train/bus leaves from each location. The first location is displayed at the top of the table and the last location is at the bottom. Example The first train left Derby ar 11:25, got to Sheffield at 12:06, Wakefield Westgate at 12:36, Leeds at 12:54, York at 13:31 and Darlington at 14:02.
